title: Does it always settle?
objectives: Recognise periodic and reducible chains that do not converge.
State when a chain converges to a unique $\pi$ from every start.

screens.title: A chain that swaps
screens.prose: A two-state chain switches every step: $P = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. The bars show the chance of being at A and at B after $k$ steps. Slide $k$, then try other starting chances.
screens.question: Start surely at A. What does the chance of being at A do as $k$ grows?

options.why: You expected the bars to meet, as the regime chain's did. Step $k$ one at a time: A reads 1, 0, 1, 0.
You kept the start. After one step the chain is surely at B, so the A bar drops to 0.

options.text: It swings less and less, towards 0.5
options.why: You expected damped swings. Here every swing is full size: 1 at even steps, 0 at odd ones.

hints.text: Set the start to 1, then move $k$ one step at a time.

feedback.correct: Every step flips the chain, so the chance flips too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step $k$ from 0 to 4 and read the A bar each time.

explain.text: From A the chain is at A after every even number of steps and at B after every odd number. So $P^k$ is $I$ for even $k$ and $P$ for odd $k$, and never converges. Start at 0.5, though, and the bars never move.

screens.title: Count days instead
screens.prose: The chances never settle, but count days instead. From A the swap chain is at A on days 0, 2, 4 and so on. The bars show the share of the first $k$ days spent at each state.
screens.question: What share of days does the chain spend at A in the long run?

widget.label: Long-run share of days at A

hints.text: Slide the days to 40.
A gets every other day.
Half the days: 0.5.

feedback.correct: Every other day is spent at A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 40 days and read the A bar.

byKey.one: You counted the start only. The odd days are all spent at B.
byKey.zero: From A the chain is back at A on every even day.

explain.text: The share of days at A heads to $\tfrac12$, and $\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ solves $\pi P = \pi$. The chain returns to A only at even steps: it is **periodic** with period 2. A periodic chain still has a stationary $\pi$, read as a share of time.

screens.title: A small self-loop
screens.prose: Change the swap slightly. Each step the chain stays put with chance 0.1 and switches with chance 0.9: $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.1 & 0.9\\ 0.9 & 0.1\end{pmatrix}$. It starts at A. Slide $k$.
screens.question: What does the chance of being at A do now?

options.text: It swings, but the swings shrink and it settles at 0.5
It alternates for ever, like the swap
options.why: You expected a 0.1 stay chance to change nothing. Slide to $k = 20$: A reads 0.506.
0.1 is the one-step chance of staying put. It is not a long-run share.
0.9 is the one-step chance of switching. The bars settle where both states are equally likely.

hints.text: The swings around 0.5 get smaller each step.
At $k = 20$ the A bar reads 0.506, and it keeps closing in.

feedback.correct: The self-loop breaks the period, so the chain settles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $k$ to 30 and read the A bar.

explain.text: Staying put lets the chain return to A in one step, so returns are no longer locked to even steps. The chain is **aperiodic**, and $P(\text{at A}) = 0.5 + 0.5(-0.8)^k$, so the swing shrinks by 0.8 each step. At $k = 20$ that is 0.506.

screens.title: A three-step cycle
screens.prose: Periods can be longer than 2. Three states in a ring: A goes to B, B to C and C back to A, each with chance 1. The chain starts at A.
screens.question: What is $P(X_{100} = \text{A} \mid X_0 = \text{A})$?

options.why: You used the stationary share $\tfrac13$. That is the share of time at A, not the chance at one step.
The chain is back at A at multiples of 3, and 100 is not one: $100 = 3 \times 33 + 1$.
You expected the chance to shrink with time. Here the chain's position is certain at every step.

hints.text: At which steps is the chain at A?
At steps 0, 3, 6, 9 and so on.
$100 = 99 + 1$, and 99 is a multiple of 3. So step 100 is one step past A.

feedback.correct: Step 100 is one step past A, so the chain is at B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the remainder when 100 is divided by 3.

explain.text: The chain is at A exactly when $k$ is a multiple of 3, so $X_{100} = \text{B}$ for sure. Its period is 3. Still, $\pi = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ is stationary, and a third of all steps are spent at A.

screens.title: States you can reach
screens.prose: A five-state chain. A state is reachable from A if some path of arrows leads there from A.
screens.question: Tap every state the chain can visit after starting at A.

hints.text: Follow the arrows out of A, then out of each state you reach.
From A the chain can stay at A or go to B. From B it can go back to A or stay.
No arrow leaves the pair A, B. So A and B are the whole answer.

feedback.correct: From A the chain never leaves A and B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow only arrows that point away from the states you have reached.

byKey.all: You assumed every state connects to every other. No arrow leaves the pair A, B.
byKey.with-e: E points into A, but no arrow points from A or B to E. Arrows only work one way.
byKey.E: E sends the chain to A, not the other way round.
byKey.C: No arrow leads from A or B to C. Only E reaches C.
byKey.D: D is reached only through C, and C only from E.

explain.text: From A the chain can only reach A and B, since no arrow leaves that pair. A set the chain never leaves is a **closed class**. C and D form a second one, so this chain is **reducible**: not every state reaches every other.

screens.title: The start decides
screens.prose: Inside A and B the chain settles at $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$; inside C and D at $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$. So in the order A, B, C, D, E, both $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 0, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$ solve $\pi P = \pi$.
screens.question: Start at E. What is the long-run chance the chain is at B?

widget.label: Long-run chance at B, from E

hints.text: From E, which class does the chain join, and with what chance?
It joins A and B with chance 0.5, and C and D with chance 0.5.
Then it spends $\tfrac23$ of its time at B: $0.5 \times \tfrac23$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each class's long-run split by the chance the chain joins it.

byKey.inside: $\tfrac23$ is the share of B inside its class. From E the chain joins that class only half the time.
byKey.fifth: You spread the time evenly over five states. The chain leaves E at once, and the classes have their own splits.
byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance of joining A and B. Inside that class only $\tfrac23$ of the time is at B.

explain.text: From E the chain joins A and B or C and D, with chance 0.5 each, and never leaves. So its limit is $0.5(\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 0, 0, 0) + 0.5(0, 0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$, giving $\tfrac13$ at B. From A it would be $\tfrac23$, and from C it would be 0.

screens.title: One answer for every start?
screens.prose: A colleague solves $\pi P = \pi$ for this chain with software. It returns $\pi = (\tfrac16, \tfrac13, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, 0)$, in the order A, B, C, D, E. She uses it as the long-run split for every starting state.
screens.question: The chain starts at C. What is its long-run chance of being at A?

options.why: You used her $\pi$ for a start at C. From C the chain never reaches A.
That is A's share inside its own class. A start at C never enters that class.
You spread the time evenly over five states. From C the chain only visits C and D.

hints.text: Which states can the chain reach from C?
Only C and D: no arrow leaves them.
So the chance of being at A is 0 at every step.

feedback.correct: From C the chain stays in C and D for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which states are reachable from C.

byKey.unique: You assumed $\pi P = \pi$ has one solution. This chain is reducible, so it has many, and the start picks the limit.

explain.text: Her vector is one stationary distribution among many: every mix of $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23, 0, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$ works. It is the limit only for a start at E. From C the limit is $(0, 0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$.

screens.title: When it always settles
screens.prose: A chain is **irreducible** if every state can reach every other. It is **aperiodic** if returns are not locked to multiples of some $d > 1$. The theorem, stated without proof: a finite chain that is both has a unique $\pi$, and $$\pi_0 P^k \to \pi \text{ from every start } \pi_0.$$
screens.question: Which chain is sure to converge to one $\pi$ from every start?

options.why: You checked irreducible but not aperiodic. The swap has period 2, so its $P^k$ alternates.
Each state is its own closed class, so the chain is reducible. Its limit is wherever it starts.

options.text: The three-state cycle A, B, C
options.why: Every state reaches every other, but returns take multiples of 3 steps. It is periodic.

feedback.correct: Irreducible, with self-loops that break any period.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check both conditions for each chain.

explain.text: The self-loop chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so the theorem applies. The swap and the cycle fail aperiodicity; the identity fails irreducibility. Each still has a stationary distribution, but not one that attracts every start.

screens.title: Why the swap never settles
screens.prose: Prove that $P^k$ never converges for the swap $P = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, yet its time average does.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $P^{2m+1} = P^{2m}P = P$, so $P^k$ flips between $I$ and $P$ and has no limit
$\tfrac12(P^{2m} + P^{2m+1}) = \tfrac12(I + P)$, whose rows are both $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \pi$: the time average settles

hints.text: Start with the smallest power that is simple.
Even powers come from $P^2$; odd powers add one more $P$.
Square, even powers, odd powers, then average a pair.

feedback.correct: Even and odd powers differ, but their average is $\pi$ in every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one before it.

byKey.d3: Odd powers are built from the even ones, so they come after them.
byKey.d4: The average needs both the even and the odd powers.

explain.text: $P^2 = I$ makes every even power $I$ and every odd power $P$, so the sequence never settles. Averaging one even and one odd step gives $\tfrac12(I + P)$, every row of which is $\pi$. That is why $\pi$ still describes the share of time.

screens.title: A rule that flips
screens.prose: A trading rule holds Long, Flat or Short each day. After Long or Short it always goes Flat. After Flat it goes Long or Short with chance $\tfrac12$ each. It is Flat on day 0.
screens.question: Fill in the table.

hints.text: When can the rule be Flat?
Solve $\pi P = \pi$: $\pi_F = \pi_L + \pi_S$ and $\pi_L = \pi_S = \tfrac12\pi_F$.
$\pi = (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14)$. From Flat on day 0, it is Flat on every even day and never on an odd day.

feedback.correct: Flat half the time, but only ever on even days.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the share of days from the chance on one particular day.

byKey.r0c1: Solve $\pi P = \pi$ with the shares adding to 1: $\pi_F = \tfrac12$.
byKey.r1c1: You used the long-run share for one day. Day 101 is odd, and the rule is never Flat on an odd day.
byKey.r2c1: You used the long-run share for one day. Day 100 is even, and the rule is Flat on every even day.

explain.text: The rule is Flat on every even day, so $P(\text{Flat})$ flips between 1 and 0. Yet half of all days are Flat: $\pi = (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14)$. A backtest that samples only even days would see a strategy that never trades.

ideas: A periodic chain, such as the swap, still has a stationary $\pi$, but $P^k$ cycles and never converges. $\pi$ is then the long-run share of time.
A reducible chain has several closed classes and many stationary distributions. The start decides which one the chain ends in.
A finite chain that is irreducible and aperiodic has one $\pi$, and $\pi_0 P^k \to \pi$ from every start. A self-loop breaks a period.

formula.name: Convergence theorem
formula.note: For a finite chain. Irreducible alone still gives a unique $\pi$, as a share of time.

summary.trap: An alternating $P^k$ does not mean there is no $\pi$. And when the chain is reducible, a solution of $\pi P = \pi$ is not the limit from every start.

quiz.prose: For the swap chain $P = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, a student says: $P^k$ never converges, so the chain has no stationary distribution.
quiz.question: Which reply is right?

options.text: $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ is stationary; only the convergence fails

options.why: You read the alternating $P^k$ as no stationary distribution. Check $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)P = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$.

options.text: $(1, 0)$ is stationary, because the chain starts at A
options.why: One step sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$, so it is not fixed.
Each is sent to the other by one step. You mixed up periodic with reducible.

feedback.correct: A stationary distribution exists; it describes time, not one step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ in $\pi P = \pi$.

explain.text: $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)P = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, so a stationary distribution exists. What fails is $\pi_0 P^k \to \pi$, because the chain has period 2. Half of all steps are spent in each state.

quiz.question: How many closed classes does the chain have?

widget.label: Number of closed classes
widget.accept: 2: the pair 1, 2 and the single state 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group the states that reach each other and that no arrow leaves.

byKey.one: States 1 and 2 never reach 3, and 3 never reaches them. They cannot be one class.
byKey.three: 1 and 2 reach each other, so they belong to the same class.

explain.text: 1 and 2 move between themselves and never reach 3, and 3 stays put. That is two closed classes, so the chain is reducible. Both $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 1)$ are stationary.

quiz.prose: $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.2 & 0.8\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. State 2 always moves to state 1, and state 1 sometimes stays.
quiz.question: What is the long-run chance of state 1, from any start?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Balance the flows: $0.8\pi_1 = 1 \cdot \pi_2$.

byKey.half: You treated it as a swap. The self-loop at state 1 keeps the chain there a little longer.
byKey.stay: 0.2 is the one-step chance that state 1 stays. It is not a long-run share.
byKey.swap: $\tfrac49$ is the share of state 2. You used $a/(a + b)$.

explain.text: The chain is irreducible, and the self-loop at state 1 makes it aperiodic, so it converges. $0.8\pi_1 = \pi_2$ with $\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1$ gives $\pi_1 = \tfrac{1}{1.8} = \tfrac59$. The theorem says every start ends there.

quiz.prose: Four states in a ring, A to B to C to D and back to A, each with chance 1. The chain starts at A.
quiz.question: What is $P(X_{10} = \text{A})$?

options.why: You used the stationary share. That is the share of time at A, not the chance at step 10.
Returns to A come at multiples of 4, and 10 is not one.
Nothing here is random: the chain's position at each step is certain.

feedback.correct: $10 = 4 \times 2 + 2$, so the chain is at C.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 10 by the period, 4.

explain.text: The chain is at A only at steps 0, 4, 8, 12 and so on. Step 10 is two past 8, so the chain is at C. The period is 4, and $\pi = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)$ describes time only.
